     Tables read the 05/06/07 analysis parquets + the evidence spans. Action

```{r setup}
library(arrow); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(readr)
library(stringr); library(scales); library(gt); library(here); library(glue); library(jsonlite)
options(arrow.skip_nul = TRUE)

ANALYSIS <- here("phase2", "data", "analysis", "deliverable06")
OUTPUT   <- here("phase2", "output", "deliverable06")
FIGS     <- file.path(OUTPUT, "figures")

verdicts <- read_parquet(file.path(ANALYSIS, "candidate_verdicts.parquet"))
mit      <- read_parquet(file.path(ANALYSIS, "candidate_mitigation_summary.parquet"))
clusters <- read_parquet(file.path(ANALYSIS, "ce_clusters.parquet"))
ce_land  <- read_parquet(file.path(ANALYSIS, "ce_landscape_ces.parquet"))
corp     <- read_parquet(file.path(ANALYSIS, "candidate_corpus.parquet"))
facts    <- read_parquet(file.path(ANALYSIS, "candidate_facts.parquet"))
inv      <- read_parquet(file.path(ANALYSIS, "fonsi_project_inventory.parquet"))
enr      <- read_parquet(file.path(ANALYSIS, "fonsi_enrichment.parquet")) |>
  filter(!is.na(action_summary)) |> mutate(is_mit = is_mitigated_fonsi %in% TRUE)
n_mit_dep_case <- sum(enr$is_mit & enr$mitigation_dependence == "case_specific_dependent", na.rm = TRUE)
n_mit_noncand  <- sum(enr$is_mit & !(as.character(enr$project_id) %in%
                                     as.character(filter(corp, is_fonsi)$project_id)))

corp_fonsi  <- corp |> filter(is_fonsi)
n_clean     <- inv |> filter(project_energy_type == "Clean") |> distinct(project_id) |> nrow()
n_candidate <- corp_fonsi |> distinct(project_id) |> nrow()
n_ce_shaped <- corp_fonsi |> filter(is_profile_subtype) |> distinct(project_id) |> nrow()
n_other     <- n_clean - n_candidate

n_new   <- sum(verdicts$verdict == "new")
n_adopt <- sum(verdicts$verdict == "adopt")
n_ce    <- nrow(ce_land)
n_units <- n_distinct(ce_land$agency_unit)
n_xdup  <- sum(ce_land$xagency_near_duplicate, na.rm = TRUE)
n_xclust <- sum(clusters$n_agencies >= 2)
n_bounds <- sum(ce_land$states_any_bound, na.rm = TRUE)
tx_mit  <- mit$mitigated_share[mit$candidate_category == "transmission_upgrade"]

cstats        <- read_parquet(file.path(ANALYSIS, "corpus_mitigation_stats.parquet"))
n_mit_corpus  <- cstats$n_mitigated_fonsi[1]
mit_share_cor <- cstats$mitigated_share[1]
n_enf_only    <- cstats$n_enforceable_only[1]
```

## Executive Summary

::: {.callout-note}
## Key Findings

- **Every bounded, low-impact decarbonization action has a text-similar existing CE
  candidate** (pending verification). None looks net-new (`r n_new` to *develop*),
  and none exceeds a *parsed* limit in its matched CE candidate (no deterministic
  *expand* candidates under the current heuristic). The likely opportunity is to
  **adopt / harmonize** an existing CE — `r n_adopt` **candidate** adopt
  opportunities, pending CE-coverage adjudication.
- **The clearest case is transmission upgrades within existing right-of-way:**
  `r verdicts$n_profile_fonsi[verdicts$candidate_category=="transmission_upgrade"]`
  bounded, low-impact FONSIs across BLM, DOE, and the power-marketing
  administrations, for work TVA already covers under its CE #17.
- **Most decarbonization FONSIs lean on committed mitigation** — `r n_mit_corpus` of
  `r n_clean` (`r percent(mit_share_cor, 1)`) are *mitigated* FONSIs, so a CE built
  from them must **encode the recurring mitigations as design criteria**, not rely
  on case-by-case commitments.
- **Adopting a peer agency's CE is well-precedented:** of `r comma(n_ce)` existing
  federal CEs, `r n_xclust` action-families are already shared across two or more
  agencies.
- **Net-new CEs most likely lie outside this candidate set** — in the
  ~`r n_other` decarbonization FONSIs not yet categorized (the recommended next step).
:::

This report delivers:

> Technical support for new regulatory categorical exclusion development:
> identifying patterns in FONSIs.

Under CEQ's April 2026 CE guidance, a prior Environmental Assessment that ended in
a **Finding of No Significant Impact (FONSI)** is explicit, citable substantiation
for a CE — so recurring decarbonization FONSIs are the natural evidence base for new,
expanded, or adopted categorical exclusions.

> **Method note.** Action definitions, numeric limits (acreage, line length,
> voltage, well count), and the mitigation read now come from a one-pass LLM
> enrichment of all 451 decarbonization FONSIs (Claude Sonnet), with every quoted
> value verified verbatim against its cited source page (97% verified). The
> CE-coverage match remains a ranking aid pending eCFR confirmation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Methodology

The deliverable runs **three analyses, each on a different data source.** They are
not a single funnel — only Analysis 1 starts from the full FONSI corpus; Analysis
2 works from the mitigated subset of it, and Analysis 3 works from the existing
federal CE catalog (not FONSIs at all).

| Analysis | Data source | Scope |
|---|---|---|
| **1 · Scaling CEs (develop, expand, or adopt)** | Decarb EAs with FONSIs | `r n_ce_shaped`/`r n_clean` projects (~`r percent(n_ce_shaped / n_clean, 1)`) |
| **2 · Mitigated FONSIs** | Decarb Mitigated FONSIs | `r n_mit_corpus` of `r n_clean` projects (`r percent(mit_share_cor, 1)`) |
| **3 · Current federal CE catalog** | Existing federal CE catalog | `r comma(n_ce)` CEs |

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
### Steps for each analysis

**Analysis 1 · Scaling CEs**

1. **Data —** the `r n_clean` decarbonization EA→FONSI projects. A FONSI concludes a full Environmental Assessment, so each is a documented federal "no significant impact" determination — the evidence base for a CE.
2. **Sort** each FONSI into a candidate action type (transmission upgrades, solar, geothermal exploration) by keyword and technology.
3. **Keep the bounded, low-impact subset** within each type — the small, routine projects that could plausibly be a CE (in-corridor upgrades, not major rebuilds).
4. **Match** each candidate against the existing federal CE catalog by text similarity.
5. **Read** the matched CE's stated size limits (acres, miles, kV, MW, wells), where it has any.
6. **Classify** as **develop** (no existing CE covers it), **expand** (our FONSIs exceed the CE's stated limit), or **adopt** (a CE exists, but at a different agency than the ones doing these FONSIs).

**Analysis 2 · Mitigated FONSIs**

1. **Data —** the mitigated FONSIs: the subset whose "no significant impact" finding depends on committed mitigation rather than the action being inherently low-impact (`r n_mit_corpus` of `r n_clean`, `r percent(mit_share_cor, 1)`).
2. **Flag** each FONSI's mitigation dependence from the LLM read — *case-specific-dependent* (the finding rests on committed mitigation) vs *design-feature-only* (inherently bounded) vs *none*.
3. **Measure** the mitigated share and the resource areas where mitigation recurs, within each action type.
4. **Read for CE design —** a mitigation that recurs consistently across a class is a codifiable CE design criterion; an idiosyncratic one is a disqualifier.

**Analysis 3 · Current federal CE catalog**

1. **Data —** the existing federal CE catalog (the [CE Explorer export](https://ce.permitting.innovation.gov/) — `r comma(n_ce)` CEs across `r n_units` agency units, each linking to its eCFR source).
2. **Compare** every CE to every other by text similarity.
3. **Flag** near-duplicates that recur at more than one agency.
4. **Group** those into shared "action families."
5. **Read** each CE's stated numeric limits, where it has any → what is already covered and how routinely agencies share the same CE (the precedent for *adopt*).
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Analysis 1 — Scaling CEs (develop, expand, adopt)

> **Every bounded, low-impact decarbonization action already has a text-similar
> existing CE at another agency.** None looks net-new (`r n_new` to *develop*) and
> none exceeds a stated CE limit (0 to *expand*) — so all `r n_adopt` resolve to
> **adopt**: agencies are running full EAs on actions a peer agency already
> categorically excludes (pending eCFR confirmation of each match).

## The four candidates, ranked by match to an existing CE

Each action already has a categorical exclusion at another agency. Ordered by how
closely it matches that existing CE (highest similarity first):

1. **Solar (CE-shaped subset)** — adopt the small-solar CE held by the **Department
   of Energy** (`DOE-1--5-87`), for bounded projects on previously disturbed land.
2. **Temporary resource assessment** — adopt the site-characterization CE held by the
   **Department of Energy** (`DOE-1--3-43`), for surveys, stream gauges, and borings.
3. **Geothermal exploration** — adopt the exploration-drilling CE held by the
   **Department of Energy** (`DOE-1--3-43`), for slim-hole / temperature-gradient wells.
4. **Transmission upgrades** — adopt the routine-maintenance CE held by the
   **Tennessee Valley Authority** (`TVA #17`), so BLM, DOE, NNSA, and the
   power-marketing administrations can stop running full EAs for in-corridor work.

## The outcome at a glance

The `r n_clean` decarbonization FONSIs split three ways (colors match the figure):

- **Bounded, low-impact → adopt** — the `r n_ce_shaped` projects in a recurring action
  type *and* small/routine enough to be CE-shaped. **Every one resolves to adopt** —
  none net-new to *develop*, none exceeding a CE limit to *expand*.
- **Recurring type, broader** — the `r n_candidate - n_ce_shaped` projects in a recurring
  type but too large to be a CE (major rebuilds, greenfield).
- **Not a recurring type** — the `r n_other` uncategorized projects: the net-new search
  pool (Analysis 3).

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-outcomes
#| fig-cap: "The decarbonization FONSI universe, split into the uncategorized pool, the broader recurring-type projects, and the bounded actions that resolve to adopt."
#| out-width: 96%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_outcomes.png"))
```

## Steps 1–2 · Sorting the FONSIs into action types

Every decarbonization FONSI is sorted into one of **five recurring action types**
(transmission upgrades, solar, geothermal exploration, onshore wind, temporary
resource assessment), or a sixth **catch-all** — the `r n_other` FONSIs that don't fit
a recurring pattern (the net-new search pool, examined in Analysis 3). Within each
recurring type we then split:

- **Bounded, low-impact** (teal) — the small, routine version that could plausibly be
  a CE: in-corridor work, short segments, previously disturbed land, no major new
  construction. *These are what we carry forward.*
- **Broader** (grey) — the larger or greenfield projects (major rebuilds, new
  corridors, utility-scale greenfield). Set aside; not CE-shaped.

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-sorting
#| fig-cap: "Every decarbonization FONSI by action type; teal = the bounded, low-impact subset kept for matching, grey = broader projects set aside."
#| out-width: 94%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_action_distribution.png"))
```

## Step 3 · Matching to the existing CE catalog

Each **candidate action type** — e.g. *geothermal exploration*, the cluster of bounded
geothermal-drilling FONSIs, summarized by its defining terms — is compared against all
`r comma(n_ce)` existing federal CEs to find the closest one. The similarity score runs
**0 to 1** and blends two signals: *semantic* similarity (do the texts mean the same
thing?) and *word overlap* (do they share the key terms?). **It is not a percent of
matching text** — it's a cosine-style similarity.

So what counts as a *strong* match? First set a **baseline**: how similar is a candidate
to a *random, unrelated* CE? Almost always tiny — about **0.07**, and rarely above **0.20**
(the grey band in the figure). Measured against that floor, the best matches —
**0.45 to 0.67** — are **several times higher**: genuinely close, on-topic matches, not
coincidence. For example, geothermal exploration matches a DOE exploration-drilling CE at
**0.50** (sharing *geothermal, exploration, well, temperature gradient*); solar matches a
DOE solar CE at **0.67**, the strongest of the four.

The score is a **ranking aid, not the verdict** — it surfaces the closest CE, but the
actual develop-vs-adopt call is made by **confirming that CE against its eCFR text**.
No candidate is anywhere near the unrelated-CE baseline, so none resolves to *develop*.

```{r ce-match-table}
verdicts |>
  filter(verdict != "contrast") |>
  arrange(desc(best_ce_match_score)) |>
  transmute(
    Action = str_replace(candidate_label, " \\(.*\\)", ""),
    `Closest existing CE (held by)` = paste0(best_ce_structured_id, " (", best_ce_agency, ")"),
    Similarity = sprintf("%.2f", best_ce_match_score)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "How each candidate matched the existing CE catalog",
             subtitle = "Closest existing CE by text similarity (a ranking aid, not verified coverage)") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(12))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-ce-match
#| fig-cap: "Best-match similarity to an existing CE, per candidate (dashed line = the soft 0.40 reference)."
#| out-width: 84%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_ce_match.png"))
```

## Step 3 · How big are the bounded projects?

A categorical exclusion usually carries a size limit — *"up to N miles," "fewer than X
wells."* To see what such a limit would look like for these actions, we read the sizes
the bounded FONSIs actually report. Each box below is one metric's range across the
bounded subset: transmission upgrades are mostly **short line segments at
sub-transmission voltages**, and geothermal exploration is **a handful of wells, not
dozens**. That observed range is what a new or adopted CE would set its threshold
against. (None of the matched CEs state a limit our FONSIs exceed, so nothing resolves
to *expand*.)

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-sizes
#| fig-cap: "The size range of the bounded FONSIs by metric — the box is the median and middle 50%, whiskers the range, dots the individual FONSIs."
#| out-width: 92%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_sizes.png"))
```

## Step 4 · Classifying, then ranking

**First, classify** each candidate with a three-question rule:

1. **Is there a close existing CE?** No → **develop** a new one. *(None here — every match clears the baseline.)*
2. **Does a close CE exist, but our FONSIs exceed its stated size limit?** Yes → **expand** that CE. *(None here — no matched CE states a limit our projects exceed.)*
3. **Does a close CE exist, but at a *different* agency than the ones doing these FONSIs?** Yes → **adopt** it. *(All four land here.)*

So all four candidates classify as **adopt**. The figure below is the *second* step —
**ranking** the four adopts so you know which to pursue first. Each gets a transparent
score (0–1) summing six factors; the bar length is the priority and the colors show why:

- **Novelty** — a brand-new CE (develop) outranks expanding or adopting one.
- **Volume** — how many bounded FONSIs back it (more evidence ranks higher).
- **Agency/state spread** — how widely the action recurs (broader = more agencies benefit).
- **Has size limits** — whether we can state a numeric bound (easier to write the CE).
- **Low mitigation dependence** — less reliance on case-by-case mitigation (a cleaner CE).
- **Profile candidate** — a small bonus for being a core recurring subtype.

So transmission ranks first not because it matches a CE most closely (it doesn't — solar
does), but because it has **the most FONSIs across the most agencies and states**.

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-classification
#| fig-cap: "Each candidate's rank score, broken into its six contributing factors (bar length = total priority)."
#| out-width: 92%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_classification.png"))
```

## Timing · do these EAs predate the FRA?

The 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act (FRA, June 2023) gave agencies explicit authority
to **adopt another agency's categorical exclusion** — the exact move this analysis
recommends. So the age of these EAs matters. Using decision dates **merged from the
D4 timeline**, **all but one** of the dated bounded FONSIs were decided *before* the
FRA — these agencies ran full EAs without the adoption shortcut now available. (Dates
are known for ~⅔ of the bounded set; the rest are undated in the D4 output.)

This cuts two ways. **It is a real limitation:** the corpus is almost entirely pre-FRA,
so we cannot see whether agencies have *already* started adopting these CEs since June
2023 — the recent picture may differ, and that bounds how current these specific
opportunities are. **But it also sharpens the recommendation:** these agencies ran full
EAs precisely because, at the time, the streamlined adoption path did not exist. Now that
the FRA provides it, adopting the existing CE is exactly the efficiency the record points
to. The clear next step is to refresh the corpus with post-FRA EAs and check whether the
shift is already underway.

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-timeline
#| fig-cap: "The bounded FONSIs by decision year (D4 timeline), relative to the FRA's June 2023 CE-adoption authority."
#| out-width: 88%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_timeline.png"))
```

## Worked example: transmission upgrades within existing right-of-way

The strongest-evidenced case:
**`r verdicts$n_profile_fonsi[verdicts$candidate_category=="transmission_upgrade"]`
bounded, low-impact FONSIs** for in-corridor transmission upgrades (reconductoring,
component replacement, minor rebuilds), across **BLM, DOE, NNSA, and the
power-marketing administrations** in
**`r verdicts$n_states[verdicts$candidate_category=="transmission_upgrade"]`
states**. The **Tennessee Valley Authority already holds a CE** for this class of
work — *TVA CE #17, "Routine modification, repair, and maintenance of, and minor
upgrade of and addition to, existing transmission infrastructure…"*

The table below lists sample FONSIs with a **verbatim excerpt from the cited
record**, the document it came from (EA or FONSI), and the page — so each row is
directly verifiable against the source.

```{r transmission-example}
# Verified action quotes come straight from the LLM enrichment (candidate_facts.quoted_span):
# each was checked verbatim against the cited EA/FONSI page, so no span re-scraping is needed.
scope_rx <- "(?i)(replace|rebuild|reconductor|construct|install|upgrad|line|conductor|right.of.way|pole|structure|propos)"
drop_rx  <- "(?i)(finding of no significant|revision sheet|table of contents|environmental assessment$)"

ex <- facts |>
  filter(candidate_category == "transmission_upgrade", is_profile_subtype,
         !is.na(quoted_span), nchar(quoted_span) >= 50,
         str_detect(quoted_span, scope_rx), !str_detect(quoted_span, drop_rx)) |>
  distinct(project_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  left_join(corp_fonsi |> select(project_id, project_title, lead_agency_harmonized), by = "project_id") |>
  mutate(
    Source = ifelse(str_detect(tolower(citation_document_role), "fonsi"), "FONSI", "EA"),
    Agency = str_squish(str_remove_all(lead_agency_harmonized, '[\\[\\]"]')),
    Excerpt = paste0("“", str_squish(str_trunc(quoted_span, 150, ellipsis = "…")), "”")
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(Source == "FONSI"), nchar(project_title)) |>
  slice_head(n = 6)

ex |>
  transmute(
    Project = str_trunc(project_title, 44),
    `Project ID` = project_id,
    Agency,
    `Source & page` = paste0(Source, ", p. ", citation_page),
    Excerpt
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Sample transmission-upgrade FONSIs — verifiable excerpts",
             subtitle = "Verbatim, quote-verified text from the cited EA/FONSI; look up by project ID") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(11)) |>
  cols_width(`Project ID` ~ px(180), Excerpt ~ px(360))
```

*(Size limits — line length, voltage, acreage, well count — now come from the
LLM enrichment pass, which separates the disturbance footprint from study-area
figures and keeps voltage distinct from length. Each value is a structured field
backing the verdicts above, with its quote verified against the source.)*

# Analysis 2 — Mitigated FONSIs

A FONSI can mean two different things: the action is **inherently low-impact**, or
it reaches "no significant impact" **only because the applicant committed to
mitigation**. That distinction is central to CE development — a CE cannot lean on
case-by-case mitigation, so if an action's FONSIs are routinely *mitigated*, a
defensible CE for it must **bake those recurring mitigations in as design criteria**.

## How "mitigated" was determined

This is **not** an embedding or similarity model — it is the per-FONSI reading from
the **one-pass LLM enrichment (Claude Sonnet)**, the same pass used throughout the
deliverable. For every one of the 451 FONSIs the model read the finding and the
committed conditions and set two fields:

- **`is_mitigated_fonsi`** — does the "no significant impact" finding *depend* on
  committed mitigation, or is the action inherently low-impact?
- **`mitigation_dependence`** — `none` / `design_feature_only` /
  `case_specific_dependent` / `permit_or_consultation_condition` / `monitoring_only` /
  `unclear`.

The supporting mitigation text is captured **verbatim and 97%-quote-verified**, and
each FONSI is tagged with the **resource areas** its mitigation addresses (biological,
water, cultural…) from a fixed vocabulary, so we can measure which recur.

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-mitigated-overall
#| fig-cap: "How many of the decarbonization FONSIs reach 'no significant impact' only with committed mitigation."
#| out-width: 96%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_mitigated_overall.png"))
```

## This spans the whole corpus, not just the candidates

The mitigated pattern is **corpus-wide**: **`r n_mit_corpus` of `r n_clean`
(`r percent(mit_share_cor, 1)`)** decarbonization FONSIs are mitigated, and
**`r n_mit_noncand`** of those fall *outside* the five Analysis-1 candidate
types — so this is not a candidate-only artifact. By action type (including the large
*Other* pool, which is 61% mitigated):

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-mitigated-share
#| fig-cap: "Mitigated-FONSI share by action type across all 451 FONSIs — not limited to the Analysis-1 candidates."
#| out-width: 86%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_mitigated_share.png"))
```

## The dependence is overwhelmingly case-specific

Of the **`r n_mit_corpus` mitigated FONSIs, `r n_mit_dep_case` are
case-specific-dependent** — the finding rests on project-specific mitigation, not on
the action being inherently low-impact.

> **One honest caveat.** `is_mitigated_fonsi` and `mitigation_dependence` are
> *near-equivalent judgments*: the model almost always pairs "the finding depends on
> mitigation" with "that mitigation is project-specific." So this is **one consistent
> signal, not two independent confirmations.** The FONSIs it reads as inherently
> low-impact (design-feature-only or none) are exactly the ones it flags as *not*
> mitigated. The substantive finding stands: **when a FONSI leans on mitigation, that
> mitigation is tailored to the project — not a standard, transferable design feature.**
> The word cloud below is the direct evidence for that.

## Examples: the committed mitigation

So you can verify the read, here are verbatim mitigation summaries the model extracted
(each tagged case-specific-dependent):

```{r mitigation-examples}
enr |>
  filter(is_mit, !is.na(mitigation_summary), nchar(mitigation_summary) > 80) |>
  arrange(desc(nchar(mitigation_summary))) |>
  distinct(project_title, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  transmute(
    Project = str_trunc(str_squish(project_title), 38),
    `Committed mitigation (verbatim summary)` = str_trunc(str_squish(mitigation_summary), 240)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Sample committed-mitigation summaries",
             subtitle = "Verbatim from the cited FONSI/EA — the basis for the case-specific-dependent flag") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(11)) |>
  cols_width(Project ~ px(170))
```

## The mitigation language is project-specific

Why is the dependence "case-specific"? Because the measures themselves are written
**per project** — SHPO consultation here, raptor-nest buffers there, site-specific
erosion plans elsewhere. In the most-frequent words across all `r n_mit_corpus`
mitigated FONSIs' summaries, **no single term dominates**:

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-mitigation-wordcloud
#| fig-cap: "Most-frequent words in the committed-mitigation summaries of the mitigated FONSIs — the long tail of specific terms is the point."
#| out-width: 90%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_mitigation_wordcloud.png"))
```

That spread is the CE-design challenge made visible: a CE **cannot copy any one
project's measures.** What *does* recur is the **resource area** the mitigation
protects — consistently **biological, soils, water, and cultural** — and those are
what a defensible CE would distill into standing design criteria.

```{r mitigation-table}
mit |>
  left_join(verdicts |> select(candidate_category, candidate_label, verdict), by = "candidate_category") |>
  filter(verdict != "contrast") |>
  arrange(desc(mitigated_share)) |>
  transmute(
    Action = str_replace(candidate_label, " \\(.*\\)", ""),
    `FONSIs examined` = n_focus,
    `Mitigated` = n_mitigated_fonsi,
    `Mitigated share` = percent(mitigated_share, accuracy = 1),
    `Recurring resource areas` = str_trunc(top_mitigation_resource_areas, 64)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Mitigated-FONSI pattern, by candidate action type",
             subtitle = "The recurring resource areas are the codifiable part — what a CE would encode as design criteria") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(12))
```

## Boundary language: where agencies drew the significance line

Alongside mitigation, the enrichment captures the agency's explicit
**significance-threshold** statements — *"would be significant if it exceeded X," "an
EIS would be required unless Y."* Those sentences are a CE's natural numeric bounds.
Each is a verbatim, span-verified quote; real examples:

```{r boundary-examples}
first_threshold <- function(j) {
  x <- tryCatch(fromJSON(j, simplifyVector = FALSE), error = function(e) list())
  for (t in x) {
    s <- if (is.null(t$statement)) "" else t$statement
    if (nchar(s) > 45 && grepl("significan|exceed|\\bEIS\\b|threshold|not to exceed|provided|unless|greater than",
                               s, ignore.case = TRUE))
      return(s)
  }
  ""
}
enr |>
  filter(!is.na(significance_thresholds), significance_thresholds != "[]") |>
  mutate(stmt = vapply(significance_thresholds, first_threshold, character(1))) |>
  filter(nchar(stmt) > 45) |>
  distinct(project_title, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  transmute(
    Project = str_trunc(str_squish(project_title), 34),
    `Significance-threshold statement (verbatim)` = str_trunc(str_squish(stmt), 200)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Where agencies drew the significance line",
             subtitle = "Verbatim threshold statements — candidate numeric/qualitative bounds for a CE") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(11)) |>
  cols_width(Project ~ px(150))
```

These are candidate CE bounds straight from the agencies' own findings — the
thresholds a new or adopted CE would be written to stay within.

# Analysis 3 — Current-CE analysis

To know whether an action is "develop," "expand," or "adopt," we first mapped the
**entire existing federal CE body**: `r comma(n_ce)` categorical exclusions across
`r n_units` agency units, embedded and compared to one another.

```{r}
#| label: fig-d6-ce-by-agency
#| fig-cap: "The existing CE landscape — categorical exclusions by agency (top 12 of 78 units)."
#| out-width: 90%
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(FIGS, "fig_d6_ce_by_agency.png"))
```

## Numeric bounds in existing CEs

Only **`r n_bounds` of `r comma(n_ce)` CEs state a numeric limit** (acres, miles,
kV, MW); the rest are qualitative. So an "expand the stated limit" argument has
few existing precedents to lean on — part of why nothing resolved to *expand* in
Analysis 1.

## Cross-agency duplication

**`r n_xdup` CEs are near-identical to a CE at a *different* agency**, forming
**`r n_xclust` action-families shared across two or more agencies.** Adopting a
peer agency's CE is not unusual — it is how the existing landscape already works.

```{r cluster-table}
clusters |>
  filter(n_agencies >= 2) |>
  arrange(desc(n_agencies), desc(n_ces)) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  transmute(
    `Shared action (representative CE text)` = str_trunc(representative_desc, 76),
    `# agencies` = n_agencies,
    Agencies = str_trunc(agencies, 56)
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = "Action categories already excluded by multiple agencies",
             subtitle = glue("{n_xclust} cross-agency CE families in the existing catalog")) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(12))
```

The largest shared families are administrative (procurement, personnel, routine
maintenance) — which is the point: when an action is genuinely low-impact,
agencies converge on the same CE. The decarbonization actions in Section 1 are
simply ones where that convergence **hasn't happened yet**.

## Where net-new CEs would come from

Net-new CEs are empty here *by construction*: the candidate action types we
hand-picked are all well-trodden, so all are already CE'd. But of the `r n_clean`
decarbonization FONSIs, only `r n_candidate` fell into those types — the remaining
**~`r n_other`** are *other* decarbonization actions we have not yet categorized.
**Net-new CEs most likely live there.** The recommended next step is to cluster
those un-categorized FONSI action descriptions to surface recurring categories
nobody has hand-picked.

# Caveats & next steps

- **LLM-extracted, verified facts.** Action definitions, numeric limits, mitigation
  dependence, and significance thresholds come from a one-pass enrichment of all
  451 decarbonization FONSIs (Claude Sonnet); every quoted value was checked verbatim
  against its cited source page (97% verified). Values that did not verify are
  flagged, not shown.
- **CE matches are a ranking aid, not verified coverage.** Confirm each candidate
  CE against its eCFR text before acting on it — this is the one remaining
  verification step.
- **Recommended next steps:** (1) verify the `r n_adopt` adopt matches against the
  eCFR CE text; (2) cluster the ~`r n_other` un-categorized decarbonization FONSIs to
  search for net-new CEs.

**For CATF:** tell us which adopt opportunities to pursue, and whether to launch
the net-new search — and we fold your direction into the next iteration.

# Reproduction

Run from the repository root in the `nepa` conda environment:

``` bash
conda run -n nepa python phase2/code/deliverable06/_run.py
quarto render phase2/reports/deliverable06.qmd
```

`_run.py` executes the numbered chain `01`→`08` (the `08_analyze.R` figures step
needs `Rscript`). Outputs are written to:

-   `phase2/data/analysis/deliverable06/` — analysis parquets (verdicts, mitigation, CE landscape/clusters)
-   `phase2/output/deliverable06/` — `figures/`, the slim comparison table, and `review/` drill-down tables
